This research assesses the effectiveness of quantum annealing techniques for clustering particles into jets in electron-positron collisions by optimizing the 'thrust' parameter. The results indicate that quantum annealing achieves comparable results to classical exact methods and traditional classical heuristics, although optimal performance is dependent on parameter fine-tuning. However, if parameter fine-tuning is unnecessary, a hybrid quantum and classical approach may also yield similar outcomes.

Our proposed model, cross-view transformers, is a highly efficient attention-based approach to semantic segmentation from multiple camera perspectives. By utilizing a camera-aware cross-view attention mechanism, it implicitly maps individual camera views into a unified map-view representation. Each camera view incorporates intrinsic and extrinsic calibration information through positional embeddings, allowing transformers to learn the mapping without explicitly modeling geometric transformations. The architecture combines convolutional image encoders for each view with cross-view transformer layers to generate map-view semantic segmentations. Cross-view transformers offers simplicity, ease of parallelization, and real-time execution capabilities. It outperforms current state-of-the-art models on the nuScenes dataset while providing 4x faster inference speeds.

Cellular processes such as cell division and movement heavily rely on the patterns of proteins within cells. As cell shapes change, these patterns can be influenced in turn, creating a complex interplay between cell geometry and chemical reactions. Despite extensive computational studies, the mechanisms behind these dynamics are still not fully understood. We developed a conceptual model to investigate cell polarity on a dynamic cell surface, using mathematical concepts from differential geometry to derive equations governing chemical reactions on a changing cell membrane. Analyzing these equations, we discovered that changes in cell membrane shape can trigger pattern-forming instabilities in specific areas of the membrane, suppressing or shifting existing patterns. We were able to explain our findings by applying a theory of local equilibria to chemical reactions on the cell membrane, allowing us to establish a simple criterion for when geometry-induced pattern-forming instabilities occur. The interplay between cell membrane shape and chemical reactions results in a diverse array of patterns, including oscillations and waves that are not seen in static cell membranes. Our research shows that the shape of the cell membrane plays a critical role in controlling pattern formation in chemical reactions within cells.

Polite and figurative language has an understated aspect in natural language processing, even though it is a crucial component of everyday conversation. Investigating euphemisms is particularly challenging due to their susceptibility to language evolution, as well as variability in human perception of what constitutes a euphemism. To begin addressing this issue, it is necessary to gather and examine instances of euphemisms, so a corpus of terms that could be euphemistic along with samples from a larger corpus has been compiled, along with an additional subset of texts where these terms are used non-euphemistically. We also present the results of various analyses conducted on this corpus. Firstly, sentiment analysis on euphemistic texts reveals that the majority of terms generally decrease negative and offensive sentiment. Secondly, in a labeling task, there were cases of disagreement among humans as to whether terms should be classified as euphemistic, which we attribute to differences in interpretation, such as commonly accepted terms.

This paper examines the generalized Hyers-Ulam stability of the reciprocal functional equation. The specific equation under investigation is $f(2x+y)+f\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right) = \frac{2f(x)f(y)}{f(x)+f(y)} + \frac{2f(x+y)f(y-x)}{3f(y-x)-f(x+y)}$ in the context of non-Archimedean space through a direct analytical approach.

This study examines highly accurate three-dimensional surface recognition in smoothed particle hydrodynamics for unobstructed surface movements. To enhance detection precision, a novel geometric approach was first created to identify unobstructed surface particles within intricate flows. This method involves continuously scanning the area within a spherical zone centered on a particle, focusing on a conical region whose vertex is at the particle location. A particle is classified as an unobstructed surface particle if a conical region devoid of neighboring particles exists. Subsequently, a more efficient semi-geometric method was proposed, grounded in the geometric approach, to decrease computational expenses. It involves identifying nearby surface particles through positional divergence, then applying the geometric method to detect and identify unobstructed surface particles. The effectiveness and reliability of the suggested method are demonstrated by testing it on several theoretical examples.

I investigate six novel tests of general relativity through observation. Firstly, I find that a massive black hole merger's gravitational wave pulse would increase Earth's orbit around the sun by a minute amount. This effect, although tiny, is detectable and could be measured by lunar ranging methods. Secondly, I establish that general relativity imposes a maximum limit on the energy flux emitted by cosmic sources based on their redshift. Next, I consider the feasibility of intergalactic travel by modified inertia at low accelerations. According to an alternative to dark matter, modified Newtonian dynamics reduces matter's inertia at very low accelerations. I show that spacecraft operating at these conditions might make intergalactic travel possible with moderate fuel usage. Fourthly, I find that in modified Newtonian dynamics, the observed dipole of the cosmic microwave background could be attributed to primordial fluctuations. Fifthly, I demonstrate that the Milky Way's tidal gravitational forces can remove hypothetical dark matter from its satellite galaxies through quantum tunneling. Lastly, I show that a charged particle can be accelerated to infinite energy by sustaining resonance with a gravitational wave propagating along a uniform magnetic field, resulting in potential electromagnetic radiation near gravitational-wave sources.

The biadjoint scalar partial amplitude $m_n(\mathbb{I},\mathbb{I})$ can be calculated using a novel integral approach over the positive tropical Grassmannian, resulting in a global Schwinger parameterization. This work introduces a limiting procedure for all partial amplitudes $m_n(\alpha,\beta)$, leading to an indicator function-based representation in the integrand. This same procedure enables a Dirac delta function-based representation for $\phi^4$ amplitudes, which can be decomposed into $\textrm{C}_{n/2-1}$ regions, corresponding to the $q^{\rm th}$-Catalan number. Each region's contribution is associated with the $m_{n/2+1}(\alpha,\mathbb{I})$ amplitude. A combinatorial framework based on non-crossing chord diagrams is proposed for the regions, and a general formula for $\phi^4$ amplitudes using Lagrange inversion is presented. This work also initiates the investigation of $\phi^p$ theories, revealing that their regions are represented by non-crossing $(p-2)$-chord diagrams, and the structure of their expansions resembles that of Green functions in terms of connected Green functions in the planar limit of $\Phi^{p-1}$ matrix models. Potential connections to constructions based on Stokes polytopes and accordiohedra are also discussed.

A theoretical study on the spatial characteristics of two identical four-wave mixing signals produced by Gaussian beams in a thin two-level atomic sample has been conducted. Our research considers the complete spatial and spectral properties of the relevant nonlinear susceptibility parameters. This analysis has led to the identification of two key findings. Firstly, the overall power of the incident beams influences the cross-sectional shape of the four-wave mixing signals upon exiting the medium and during their free propagation. Secondly, the spectral properties of the medium impact the longitudinal distribution of the two generated signals during free propagation. We propose that the first effect arises from the saturation of the medium in regions of high intensity, whereas the second effect stems from a nonlinear refractive index contribution within the atomic medium. Notably, these effects can exhibit symmetry between the two signals, with asymmetries emerging due to differences in the detuning of the incident fields from the atomic resonance.

A novel strategy is developed to design a suitable polarizability distribution for a metasurface aperture that can generate a target radiation pattern. The metasurface aperture is composed of subwavelength metamaterial elements, each functioning as a small radiating, polarizable dipole. To identify the optimal polarizability distribution, a holographic approach is employed to first derive the necessary aperture fields, which can then be converted to a polarizability distribution using electromagnetic equivalence principles. However, the inherent properties of a single passive metamaterial resonator restrict its polarizability magnitude and phase to a limited range. To address this limitation, a set of transformations is introduced that map the ideal polarizability distribution to the feasible distribution, facilitating the design of optimized beam patterns for metasurface antennas. These transformations can be easily visualized and implemented, and several examples are presented, along with numerical simulations to validate the proposed design approach.

Developing next-generation surgical devices and workflow monitoring systems heavily relies on advancing activity recognition in surgical videos. Given the variable duration of surgeries, two-stage deep learning models, consisting of a backbone and temporal sequence component, are commonly applied to analyze these videos. In this study, we evaluated multiple cutting-edge backbones and temporal models for surgical activity recognition and found that Swin-Transformer in conjunction with BiGRU temporal modeling achieved superior results. Our assessment of various datasets, including an extensive collection of over 800 surgery videos captured in multiple clinical settings, as well as smaller datasets, revealed the robustness of this approach. Furthermore, we tested its adaptability to novel domains by fine-tuning the model for use in a new hospital and employing an unsupervised domain adaptation strategy.

The latest CDF measurement of the $W$ mass at 80,433 $\pm$ 9 MeV holds the record for the most precise direct measurement. Yet, this result diverges from the Standard Model predicted mass of 80,359.1 $\pm$ 5.2 MeV by a substantial margin of $7\sigma$. CDF utilized an outdated ResBos code limited to NNLL+NLO accuracy whereas the newer ResBos2 code offers N${}^3$LL+NNLO precision. Our findings suggest that the CDF experiment's data-driven methods effectively incorporate most of the higher order corrections, and considering these corrections would at most reduce the reported value by 10 MeV.

This research addresses the issue of restoring malfunctional three-dimensional objects by considering the physical relationships between the object and the user, rather than relying solely on static object perception. Building on the human ability to mentally simulate object interactions and predict outcomes, our proposed framework FixNet integrates perception, physical dynamics, and functionality prediction to identify the most effective fixes for faulty objects. A new dataset, FixIt, consisting of 5,000 defective objects paired with repair options, was created to support this research. Experimental results demonstrate that FixNet surpasses baseline models in accuracy and maintains high performance on objects with similar interaction types.

To refine predictions of the Dirac CP-violating phase, models modifying tribimaximal or bimaximal mixing patterns have been updated and improved. Perturbations, achieved through rotations between different sectors, are applied to these patterns to yield modified mixing matrices. We then map these matrices into a standard parameterization for the neutrino mixing matrix to derive correlations between the Dirac CP-phase and the oscillation angles. Using these correlations in conjunction with existing experimental data, the permissible range of the CP-phase is constrained and its probability density is determined. Additionally, the study explores future experiment potential for detecting the perturbations analyzed and proposes a model with A4 modular symmetry that is in line with one of the perturbed scenarios and successfully fits current data on oscillation parameters.

A novel method for estimating the acoustic transfer function (ATF) between different areas is presented. This approach addresses both the ATF's physical characteristics and the direction-dependent layout of these areas. Unlike existing methods, which primarily focus on receiver regions, the proposed kernel-based interpolation technique enables ATF estimation for both source and receiver areas from a given set of measured ATF data. To improve interpolation accuracy, a new reproducing kernel Hilbert space formulation incorporating directional weights is developed. Additionally, the study investigates optimization strategies for the proposed kernel function. Computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms a method without directional weighting.

We investigated the theoretical and observed mass distributions of dijet resonances produced by excited quarks in proton-proton collisions at various energies, including 13, 14, 27, 100, 300, and 500 TeV. Our analysis in-depth explored the expected shapes at the theoretical and experimental levels and isolated the effects of the excited quark's natural width, proton parton momentum distributions, radiation, and experimental resolution within these distributions. We presented the dijet mass distributions and signal acceptance in different forms, including differential and cumulative probability distributions and a mass window centered on each resonance. Our findings revealed that for a range of resonance masses, approximately between 10% and 50% of the collision energy, the dijet mass distributions and signal acceptance remain largely consistent and unaffected by variations in resonance mass and collision energy. This research complements our previous study on the sensitivity of proton-proton colliders to dijet resonances presented at the Snowmass 2021 conference.

We introduce an unsupervised representation for a scene-generating model 
that lies between per-pixel and per-image abstraction. This representation
breaks down scenes into organized clusters of spatially-oriented "blobs"
of characteristics. A feature grid, onto which these distinct "blobs" are
placed in a differentiable manner, is decoded into a visual representation
by a generative adversarial network. Due to the consistent spatial layout of
blobs and the localized nature of convolutions, our model is able to relate
unique blobs with specific elements within a scene, thereby accurately
arranging them to represent the layout of a scene. This spontaneous behavior
is demonstrated by our model's ability to perform various tasks, such as
manipulating objects within a scene, creating realistic scenes based on
constraints, and dissecting real-world images into their constituent parts,
without requiring any explicit supervision. Our method, BlobGAN, is also
shown to surpass StyleGAN2 in image quality, as measured by FID score, on
a challenging indoor scene dataset. For further information, please refer to
our project website: https://www.dave.ml/blobgan, which includes video results
and an interactive demo.

Automating the analysis of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals using machine learning (ML) classification can be a time-efficient alternative to manual analysis performed by cardiologists. However, the interpretability of deep learning models in healthcare settings has limited their application. This study develops Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) classifiers and compares their performance with shallow models, using global and local interpretability methods to analyze their behavior. Techniques such as Partial Dependence Plots and Shapley Additive Explanations are implemented on time-series ML models, including a local technique called Gradient Weighted Class Activation Maps (Grad-Cam), which is particularly effective in explaining predictions of high-performing CNN and LSTM models. It was observed that all top-performing classifiers focus on the QRS complex when making predictions.

A recently proposed teaching model, referred to as 'No-Clash Teaching' or 'NC-Teaching', has been proven optimal with two key characteristics: it adheres to Goldman and Matthias' collusion-freeness condition and its dimension (NCTD) is smaller or equal to any other optimal teaching model. Research also demonstrated that the maximum number of concepts in a concept class defined over a domain of size n with NC-teaching dimension d is at most 2^d times the combination of n and d. The main findings of this paper include the identification of the maximum concept classes of NC-teaching dimension 1 as those that are naturally induced by tournaments and the discovery of a family of concept classes where the recursive teaching dimension (RTD) grows logarithmically in relation to the number of concepts, while the NC-teaching dimension remains constant at 1. This family of concept classes effectively distinguishes between RTD and NCTD in a notable way. Moreover, the paper presents a method of constructing this family using the probabilistic method and random tournaments. It also presents a tighter upper bound for the maximum number of concepts in a concept class with NC-teaching dimension d, which involves Johnson graphs and subgraphs without large narrow cliques.

Dark matter is thought of as a gas of massive particles that collide, interact through gravity, and transfer energy quanta. A novel nonrelativistic quantum model has been proposed for this dark matter paradigm, grounded in a recently found equation for a neutral, uncharged, and unbound particle. This theory captures the quantum phenomena occurring in the particles, determines the necessary wavelength of the energy quanta, imposes constraints on the mass of dark matter particles, and forecasts a measurable gravitational wave signature linked to dark matter halos.

The concept of an optical exciton - a pair of a photo-excited electron and hole bound together within a crystal - has been extensively used in understanding various phenomena in semiconductors. These excitons, predicted to condense, diffuse, and recombine, were previously thought to exist as distinct particles that could be identified through peaks in the linear absorption spectrum. However, this paper presents an alternative perspective, demonstrating that the electron-phonon interaction breaks down the initial optical excitons into elemental excitons, which are distinct from the original excitons and do not have the same properties caused by the induced electric field. Using a many-body perturbation theory approach and applying it to realistic systems such as monolayer MoS$_2$ and MoSe$_2$, the study reveals that the optical-elemental decomposition leads to a homogeneous broadening of absorption peaks. It is also shown that the optical excitons lose their structure and evolve into elemental excitons, which represent the true intrinsic excitations of the system and persist even after the external perturbation and induced electric fields have disappeared.

A novel formal logic system, called standpoint logic, supports a multi-angle approach in knowledge integration by considering multiple perspectives, even if they conflict with each other, rather than requiring their integration. We have developed formal calculi for handling propositional standpoint logics, which enable automated reasoning through algorithms that explore possible perspectives. By employing a new method referred to as "coloring," where a formula's components are assigned colors and proof search is conducted on the resulting representation, we have optimized the worst-case performance of these calculi. Our approach allows the validity of standpoint expressions to be determined in a certain time complexity since it can generate partial proof for any given coloring of the formula. We have also shown how all partial proofs can be combined to form a complete proof when the formula is valid and how certain partial proofs can be transformed into counterexamples when the formula is invalid.

In the field of spin torque magnetic memories, a novel mechanism has been discovered using electrically induced spin currents to control a magnetic bit. These systems often rely on a complex multilayer structure consisting of a ferromagnetic layer and a secondary layer that generates spin injection. However, a breakthrough has been achieved in a single, two-dimensional system featuring intrinsic magnetism and substantial Berry curvature. By investigating AB-stacked MoTe2/WSe2, a magnetic Chern insulator has been discovered at a specific carrier density, exhibiting a magnetic response to electric current. The system demonstrates hysteretic switching of resistivity as a function of applied current, with magnetic imaging revealing the reversal of individual magnetic domains in response to current. Furthermore, the real-space pattern of domain reversals aligns with spin accumulation near the high-Berry curvature Hubbard band edges, indicating that intrinsic spin-orbit torques drive the observed current-driven magnetic switching. This phenomenon has significant implications for the efficient control of magnetic order, as the required current density is significantly lower than previously reported in other systems.

Measurements have been made of cross-sections for the creation of boosted top quark pairs through proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV recorded by the ATLAS detector. Top quarks were observed in their hadronic decay and identified as large jets with high transverse momentum. After accounting for detector effects, the measured cross-section, adjusted for a specific decay mode and phase space, is approximately 331 plus or minus 39 fb. This value falls within the uncertainties of a prediction made by a model with next-to-leading order accuracy, while results at a lower level of particle interaction show better agreement with a model with even higher accuracy. When comparing the measured cross-sections with different theoretical models, most show reasonable agreement but one type of calculation shows generally better agreement with the data. Using a specific theory framework, the differential cross-sections were analyzed and limits were set on several parameters that describe interactions between particles.

In this research, we explore the process of quantum many-body teleportation, in which a single qubit is transmitted via a highly interconnected quantum system, facilitated by a scrambling transformation and local measurements on a small subset of qubits. Contrary to typical protocols, which necessitate a double replication of the system and reverse temporal evolution, we show that teleportation can be achieved in the 2D XY spin-$1/2$ model under more lenient conditions. The required long-distance entanglement for this teleportation is created from a model that features distinctive eigenstates known as rainbow scars. To accomplish this, we propose a specific protocol involving the preparation of a highly entangled state through the evolution of an initial product state, followed by iterative measurements and feedback control, all performed on just two qubits.

Legged robots face significant challenges in executing agile maneuvers like sprinting and rapid turns in uncontrolled environments. We have developed an end-to-end learned controller that has set a new standard for agility in the MIT Mini Cheetah, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 3.9 m/s. This system enables the robot to efficiently navigate diverse terrains, such as grass, ice, and gravel, and maintain stability in the face of unexpected disturbances. The controller is comprised of a neural network that has been trained through a combination of simulation-based reinforcement learning and a method for transferring knowledge from a simulated environment to real-world applications. This approach involves an adaptive curriculum that adjusts velocity commands and a dynamic system identification strategy. Video demonstrations of the robot's capabilities are available at https://agility.csail.mit.edu/.

Digital health passes demonstrate a lawful approach to achieving certain benefits of 'true elimination' COVID-19 treatment strategies by validating quarantine and vaccination status digitally. However, current systems face challenges related to region-based control and centralized storage of protected health information, hindering their widespread adoption. This work proposes a decentralized PHI storage and validation mechanism for digital health passes through an updated two-stage handshaking mechanism on a blockchain proof-of-stake consensus. The proposed mechanism enables universal validation with any jurisdiction, preserves individuals' right to independent movement, and safeguards their protected health information. The protocol's stability is validated through Monte-Carlo simulations under various attack scenarios.

Recent research has indicated that measuring velocity differences of wide binary stars to high precision with GAIA may offer an insightful test for theories attempting to replicate dark matter, specifically modified-gravity models such as MOND. As wide binaries should behave strictly according to Newton's law in standard dark-matter theories, while MOND-like theories yield distinctly different predictions, overcoming the various observational challenges is essential. This study updates a 2019 analysis using GAIA EDR3 data by selecting a large sample of 73,159 candidate wide binary stars and estimating their component masses using a main-sequence mass-luminosity relation. A comparison of the observed distribution of pairwise relative projected velocity versus projected separation with simulations reveals a clear peak close to Newtonian expectations accompanied by a long 'tail' possibly resulting from unresolved triple systems. To account for this, the study applies a mixture of binary, triple, and flyby populations to GR and MOND orbits, finding that standard gravity appears more likely than a specific MOND implementation, albeit without fully exploring the parameter space of triple models and MOND variations. Further GAIA releases and follow-up observations of a subset of systems to refine the triple population characterization are anticipated to make wide binaries a definitive test of GR versus MOND in the future.
This paper examines connections between the eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices and their diagonal elements.

In this research, we explore the concept of hypergraphs to model complex relationships among objects, leveraging their numerous applications in real-world dataset analysis. To address a key challenge, we introduce a novel heat diffusion process for hypergraphs and develop a polynomial-time algorithm to approximately identify bipartite components within them. Our algorithm's performance is theoretically validated and compared against the current state-of-the-art through comprehensive experiments on both artificial and actual hypergraph datasets, revealing consistent and substantial improvements over existing solutions.

The principle of entropy increase suggests that in physics, isolated systems can only see their total entropy rise but never decrease. One example of an irreversible process is a normal metal's electric current being cut off, resulting in Joule heat due to resistance. Historically, the transition of a superconductor into its normal state was thought to be an irreversible thermodynamic process. However, the Meissner effect, discovered in 1933, is an experimental finding of a process that reverses this irreversible transition. The belief in entropy's inevitable rise led physicists to reevaluate the superconducting transition, now understood as a phase change. The conventional theory of superconductivity, developed using reversible thermodynamics, contains an internal contradiction in predicting Joule heating despite describing persistent currents as being cut off by a phase change and reappearing upon returning to the superconducting state. The success of the conventional theory of superconductivity has raised doubts about the validity of the principle of entropy increase.

Researchers have recorded a prolonged, unusually high gamma-ray emission level from VER J0521+211 in 2013 and 2014, observed by various telescopes. The peak radiation intensity was approximately 37% of the Crab Nebula's flux, as recorded through nightly light curves. Simultaneous observations in X-ray, UV, and optical wavelengths were also captured, revealing a moderate connection between X-ray and gamma-ray radiation levels and an increased hardness in X-ray spectra during heightened activity. Based on gamma-ray spectra and background light models, a cautious estimate set the upper limit of the source's redshift at 0.31 or lower. Unlike the gamma-ray and X-ray bands, optical radiation levels did not increase during the studied period. The varying spectral profiles across optical to X-ray bands suggest that the synchrotron energy distribution peak may expand during flare-ups, a scenario that one-zone synchrotron self-Compton models can explain by adjusting the high-energy particle spectrum. Furthermore, the synchrotron peak frequency and jet radio morphology observed in the MOJAVE program align with VER J0521+211 being an intermediate-frequency-peaked BL Lac object.

Recent research has demonstrated the effectiveness of differentiable physics for solving complex soft-body manipulation tasks. Nevertheless, differentiable physics solvers often fail to achieve optimal solutions when faced with suboptimal initial contact points or multi-stage tasks that require dynamic contact adjustments. To overcome these challenges, a novel contact point discovery approach called CPDeform is proposed. This method leverages optimal transport techniques to seamlessly integrate with differentiable physics solvers and systematically avoid local minima. In both single-stage and multi-stage scenarios, CPDeform enables automatic contact point identification based on transport priorities. To rigorously evaluate CPDeform's efficacy, PlasticineLab-M was developed by extending the existing PlasticineLab benchmark to incorporate seven new, demanding multi-stage soft-body manipulation tasks. Experimental results indicate that CPDeform successfully guides the differentiable physics solver to achieve optimal solutions in cases where the vanilla solver is infeasible. Furthermore, CPDeform consistently outperforms or matches the manipulation performance of manual contact point adjustments.

Research findings indicate a widespread phenomenon of excessive mixing in lower-mass stars at a certain evolutionary stage. This phenomenon has primarily been attributed to thermohaline mixing. Current one-dimensional stellar evolution models account for thermohaline mixing, yet the direct use of observational data to distinguish between various mixing prescriptions has been restricted. In this study, a novel framework is introduced to enable the direct comparison of theoretical predictions and observational evidence: Carbon-to-nitrogen ratios from the SDSS-IV APOGEE survey are used as a proxy for mixing, while data from one-dimensional stellar evolution programs are used to determine a fluid parameter. This method enables the direct comparison of observed and predicted mixing trends. The results demonstrate a strong correlation between the amount of excessive mixing and the fluid parameter. Furthermore, this study reveals a consistent relationship between the fluid parameter and fundamental stellar properties across various theoretical models. It is also observed that stars with available data on mixing exhibit relatively low fluid parameters, suggesting specific regimes for future simulations. Additionally, this study supports the notion that increased mixing occurs at low fluid parameters, aligning with current thermohaline mixing models. This framework serves as a benchmark for theoretical modeling efforts, as it enables the validation not only of the amount of excessive mixing, but also of the relationships between mixing intensity and fundamental stellar properties.

We examine the characteristics of the ground-state and first radially excited four-quark mesons $X_0$ and $X_0^{\prime}$ with a diquark-antidiquark structure of $[ud][\overline{c}\overline{s}]$ and $J^{\mathrm{P} }=0^{+}$. Our goal is to determine whether the $X_0(2900)$ resonance recently discovered by the LHCb collaboration can be linked to either of these states. To this end, we consider $X_0$ and $X_0^{\prime}$ as tetraquarks formed by axial-vector or scalar diquark and antidiquark pairs, and calculate their spectroscopic parameters using the QCD two-point sum rule method and taking into account vacuum condensates up to dimension 15. For an axial-axial arrangement of $X_0^{(\prime)}$, we calculate partial widths for the decays $X_0^{(\prime)} \to D^{-}K^{+}$ and $X_0^{(\prime)} \to D^{0}K^{0}$, as well as estimate the full widths of the states $X_0^{(\prime)}$ by determining the strong couplings at the vertices $X_0^{(\prime)}DK$ using the light-cone sum rule method. Our results, $m=(2545 \pm 160)~\mathrm{MeV}$ and $m^{\prime}=(3320 \pm 120)~\mathrm{MeV}$, along with our estimates for the full widths $\Gamma_{0}=(140 \pm 29)~\mathrm{MeV}$ and $\Gamma_{0}^{\prime}=(110 \pm 25)~\mathrm{MeV}$, suggest that neither of these states can be identified as the $X_0(2900)$ resonance. Nevertheless, our predictions offer significant insight into the ground-state and radially excited diquark-antidiquark structures $X_0$ and $X_0^{\prime}$, providing a foundation for future experimental and theoretical studies.

Among future ground-based gravitational-wave detectors, the Einstein Telescope stands out due to its ability to generate a null stream, a signal-free data combination, that offers previously inaccessible noise model tests. Our analysis highlights the challenges in modeling the 2030s noise and its impact on next-generation detector performance. The Einstein Telescope's null stream effectively eradicates known detector glitches limiting contemporary gravitational-wave searches. The proposed techniques are computationally efficient and don't rely on prior knowledge about glitch models. Furthermore, the null stream allows unbiased noise power spectrum estimation for both real-time and offline data analysis, even with multiple loud signals present. This approach can be used alongside other null stream applications. However, the null-stream analysis for the Einstein Telescope and general detector networks has limitations and ongoing challenges.

Most existing simulations of low-mass red giant stars fail to replicate the location of the red giant branch luminosity bump, a feature indicative of the convective envelope's maximum extension during the first dredge-up phase. Data from asteroseismic parameters, such as the large frequency separation and the oscillation power frequency, have confirmed that incorporating convective overshoot beneath the convective envelope in models can improve the match between the predicted and observed luminosity bump positions. Nonetheless, these global parameters are not sufficient to investigate overshoot in individual stars. Mixed modes in red giants, characterized by their dual nature as acoustic and gravity modes, hold significant information about the star's internal structure, particularly near the convective boundary. Therefore, these modes can be leveraged to investigate interior processes, such as overshoot. Utilizing a grid of red giant models with diverse parameters, including mass, metallicity, surface gravity, and overshoot treatment, our findings suggest that variations in the overshoot amplitude and prescription in red giant models lead to notable differences in the evolution of their dipole mixed-mode oscillation frequencies, the average mixed-mode period spacing, and gravity mode phase offset term.

Active visual memory enables us to hold, modify, and use visual information around us.
Despite the unclear underlying neural processes, a specific neural indicator called contralateral delay activity (CDA) has been widely used to investigate working memory. To verify whether the CDA is a reliable indicator for working memory tasks, we re-examined eight existing CDA-related studies using a freely available EEG dataset.
We analyzed the raw EEG data from these eight studies with a standard method and successfully replicated their results, demonstrating the effectiveness of our automated EEG analysis pipeline in detecting the CDA signal. Our re-examination revealed some trends across the studies, and it also raised questions about how CDA changes over time, as well as its behavior during the recall stage, a gap in knowledge that previous studies had not addressed.
We also offer recommendations for ensuring the reproducibility of future studies, drawing from our experience and challenges encountered during this process.

For every connected analytic subvariety, we establish that there exists a pseudoconvex set which accommodates isometric extensions of all bounded holomorphic functions defined on the subvariety. We demonstrate that for specific varieties, consisting of two intersecting analytic disks at a single point, if all bounded scalar-valued functions can be isometrically extended to the pseudoconvex set, then so can matrix-valued functions. However, under the condition that the pseudoconvex set is the symmetrized bidisk, we find a counterexample, illustrating that not all functions can be isometrically extended in this context.

Researchers have developed nanomechanical resonators made from van der Waals materials that can serve as a tool to measure absorbed laser energy. By incorporating these resonators into a specific interferometer structure, their ability to respond to laser absorption is amplified. However, the newly introduced dependency of this enhanced response on the movement of the resonator has yet to be thoroughly examined. To fill this knowledge gap, a study has been conducted on niobium diselenide resonator membranes driven by electrical energy and attached to reflective substrates. A newly developed model, based on the principle of heat absorption through interference, has been used to explain the variations observed in the thermal response. According to this model, membranes consisting of fewer or single layers of niobium diselenide exhibit more pronounced thermal responses and greater tuning range at a specific wavelength. Additionally, the model indicates that the thickness of these membranes directly influences both the intensity and tuning range of the thermal responses, ultimately enabling the creation of highly sensitive thermometers using this novel type of van der Waals resonator technology.

Change detection using remote sensing images can identify changes of interest in co-registered images from two different times. Despite the success of deep learning-based change detection methods, they require a significant amount of labeled training data. Annotating these images is a labor-intensive and costly process, particularly for bi-temporal images that require pixel-wise comparisons. Conversely, there is a vast, readily available collection of unlabeled remote sensing imagery resulting from the increasing number of earth observation programs. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semi-supervised change detection model that utilizes unlabeled bi-temporal images to enhance the performance of existing change detection methods. By incorporating an unsupervised change detection loss in addition to a cross-entropy loss, the model constrains the change probability map of an unlabeled image pair to be consistent under small perturbations applied to the deep feature difference map obtained from the subtraction of latent feature representations. Experimental results on two widely used change detection datasets show that our semi-supervised approach can achieve performance comparable to that of supervised methods with as little as 10% of the labeled training data.

This paper outlines an experiment that employed our randomized hints method to help a theorem prover, OTTER, use hyper-resolution to derive Axiom(5) from the initial axioms Axiom(1), (2), (3), and (4) in Infinite-Valued Lukasiewicz Logic. The experiment generated a series of 30 to 60 hint sets, resulting in the identification of a particularly effective list of 30 hints out of a total of 900 possible combinations. Additionally, the study observed an unexpected rise in the number of generated clauses as the theorem prover applied our randomized hints strategy.

The distinctive spiral pattern of a spiral galaxy can be discerned through various observational markers such as interstellar dust, ionized gas electrons, molecular clouds, or atomic hydrogen in specific regions. This study employs an N-body simulation incorporating Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) to investigate the spiral pattern and the process of star formation within the gaseous component of a disk-shaped galaxy. We address several inquiries, including how galaxies appear distinct through the varying properties of their gas and whether the galaxy's spiral structure alters when viewed through different gas properties. We also examine whether simulated spiral arms change their shape and width depending on the gas property observed. Moreover, we aim to create a model that can accurately measure arm widths consistently, and determine whether this model applies uniformly across different gas properties. To resolve these questions, we have developed a technique for identifying and extracting the spiral structure within a disk galaxy. Utilizing this method, we further explore the characteristics of the spiral pattern across diverse gas properties, with a focus on star formation behavior and its relationship to the spiral structure.

Galaxies hosting Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) with distorted radio jets are often used to identify dense environments like galaxy groups and clusters, as the jets' distortion is assumed to be caused by the galaxies' movement through dense intergalactic gas. However, not all AGN jets in these environments appear distorted, leading to a question: why are some AGN jets affected more significantly by their surroundings than others? To investigate, a study examined a sample of 185 AGN with distorted jets and 191 with straight jets by identifying neighboring galaxies using an algorithm. The results show that AGN with distorted jets tend to reside in groups and clusters, while those with straight jets are more often isolated or paired. When considering only AGN in groups, bent AGN were found in halos with a greater number of galaxies. Conversely, straight AGN were more likely to be the brightest group galaxies. Groups hosting AGN with distorted jets also had a higher galaxy density than those hosting AGN with straight jets. A curious finding was that some AGN with distorted jets exist in seemingly less dense regions, possibly indicating they are embedded within cosmic web filaments. Overall, the study's results suggest that distorted jets are associated with galaxies in larger, denser, and less relaxed environments, potentially linking radio morphology to a galaxy's environment.

This study proposes a novel framework for modeling interactional communication in dyadic conversations, utilizing multimodal inputs from the speaker to predict multiple possibilities of the listener's corresponding motion. The framework combines the speaker's speech audio and motion using a cross-modal attention mechanism in a transformer architecture. Additionally, it incorporates a novel motion-encoding technique based on VQ-VAE to model realistic and non-deterministic listener motion. Our method effectively captures the complexity and unpredictability of nonverbal interactions between two individuals, while also generating realistic and synchronized 3D facial motion. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods both qualitatively and quantitatively. To facilitate further research in this area, we introduce a new, large-scale dataset of dyadic conversations, along with accompanying code, data, and video examples available at https://evonneng.github.io/learning2listen/.

Recent high-performance optical flow models often utilize finite-step recurrent updates, which simulate traditional algorithms by refining estimates iteratively. However, this approach leads to high computational and memory costs, and the models may not converge stably, ultimately resulting in decreased performance. To address these limitations, we introduce deep equilibrium (DEQ) flow estimators, which directly find the stable flow solution as an infinite-level fixed point in an implicit layer. This approach differentiates through the fixed point analytically, thus requiring minimal training memory. DEQ estimators are model-agnostic, allowing them to be applied to a wide range of state-of-the-art flow estimation models. By leveraging these DEQ estimators, we can compute flows faster using techniques like fixed-point reuse and inexact gradients, achieve 4 to 6 times lower training memory consumption than their recurrent counterparts, and obtain superior results with the same computational budget. Moreover, we propose a novel sparse fixed-point correction scheme to stabilize the DEQ estimators, resolving a longstanding challenge for these models. Our approach significantly improves state-of-the-art methods on the Sintel and KITTI datasets while offering substantial gains in computational and memory efficiency.

This paper examines two distinct opinion dynamics models, each formulated within the framework of the multi-dimensional Hagselmann-Krause model. These models capture how individuals adjust their opinions on multiple subjects based on peer influence, differing in how they select influencers. In one model, agents compare their aggregate opinions and interact only with those whose views align within a specified range of uncertainty. An alternative proof demonstrates the contractivity of this model's opinion range, revealing that agent opinions converge to a consensus or cluster only when their aggregate opinions do the same. In contrast, the other model involves agents comparing their opinions on individual topics and influencing one another if their opinions on each topic diverge by no more than a predetermined margin. Conditions have been identified under which this model exhibits the order-preservation property on individual topics, and it has been proven that the global opinion range remains non-increasing.

Recent studies have found that motion planners' effectiveness can be significantly enhanced by leveraging past experiences from a database. Traditionally, this database is queried for analogous past problems using a defined similarity metric. However, most existing works rely on basic similarity measures and struggle to generalize beyond their original dataset. To address this shortcoming, we propose a framework, FIRE, which extracts local representations of planning problems and learns a similarity metric from these components. To create training data, we introduce a self-supervised approach that identifies analogous and dissimilar pairs of local elements within past solution paths. A Siamese network is then trained using a contrastive loss function, and the similarity metric is derived from the network's latent space. We evaluate FIRE on an 8-DOF manipulator with five categories of motion planning problems, featuring sensed environments. Our results demonstrate that FIRE successfully retrieves relevant experiences which can inform and guide sampling-based planners even in problems outside its training scope, outperforming other established methods.

Accurate population distribution data is crucial for making informed decisions in areas like urban planning, disaster response, and resource allocation. To achieve this, precise population data is vital. The conventional census method is time-consuming and costly. Recent years have seen advancements in population estimation through statistical and machine learning techniques, which, however, often rely on limited or inaccessible data sets. As a result, developing and evaluating new methods is complicated. We address this challenge by introducing a large-scale, publicly accessible dataset of 98 European cities. The dataset integrates information from multiple sources, including digital elevation models, climate zone classifications, land use data, nighttime light measurements, and multi-spectral satellite imagery, along with data from the Open Street Map project. We anticipate that our dataset will be instrumental in driving research and innovation in the field of population estimation, enabling the development of more sophisticated and effective approaches.

Audio captioning, a crucial research area, seeks to generate informative descriptions of audio segments. Most current studies rely on encoder-decoder and transformer models using acoustic characteristics of audio segments as inputs to produce captions. Due to limited data and inadequate learning capabilities of existing models, additional information is necessary to generate coherent and natural language descriptions, as well as incorporating acoustic characteristics. To address these issues, a new encoder-decoder architecture is introduced that leverages both acoustic characteristics and extracted audio event labels as inputs. This proposed model utilizes pre-trained acoustic characteristics and audio event detection, and extensive experiments were conducted with varied acoustic characteristics, word embedding models, audio event label extraction methods, and implementation settings to determine the most effective combinations for audio captioning. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that combining audio event labels with acoustic characteristics enhances recognition performance, and the proposed method either surpasses or achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art models.

Brains process language and sensory information simultaneously to grasp language, and possess the key capability of generating mental images. This ability allows us to form novel abstract concepts or tangible objects and apply practical knowledge to solve complex problems in resource-scarce environments. Yet, existing NLU approaches largely focus on textual signals, failing to replicate human imagination capabilities, which limits their ability to accurately interpret and learn from sparse data. To address this, we propose the iACE model, which enables visual imagination through external knowledge transferred from highly advanced pre-trained vision-and-language models. Experimental results on GLUE and SWAG demonstrate that iACE outperforms visually-supervised models, and its success in both extreme and standard few-shot settings highlights its value in natural language understanding tasks with limited resources.

Spohn's conjecture II.3.6 and Jensen-Yau's Lecture 7 both seek to establish a general proof of universal fluctuations for hydrodynamic limits in large-scale stochastic interacting particle systems. However, recent studies suggest minimal progress has been made in the past few decades. This paper develops a general approach for deriving the Boltzmann-Gibbs principle for a diverse range of non-integrable and non-stationary interacting particle systems, addressing Spohn's conjecture and Jensen-Yau's Lecture. Crucially, our method relies on local and dynamic characteristics rather than universal assumptions about invariant measures or initial conditions, which contrasts with previous works. A specific application of our method results in the derivation of the KPZ equation as a large-scale limit of height functions for a non-stationary and non-integrable exclusion process with variable asymmetry. This outcome provides a first solution to Big Picture Question 1.6, which is significant for a type of "speed-change" model also relevant beyond the KPZ context, as previously studied in [De Masi-Presutti-Spohn-Wick '86, Funaki '18, Funaki-Handa-Uchiyama '91, Komoriya '98].

Gravitational waves are a natural consequence of Einstein's theory of general relativity, which was first introduced in 1915. The idea of gravitational waves, however, wasn't fully understood until 1960 when their existence was confirmed using the full theory of general relativity. Establishing a workable definition for gravitational waves proved to be a significant challenge, and their existence was only proven as a solution to the Einstein equations for a universe without dark energy. Although considerable work has been done to extend this proof to include a positive cosmological constant, a full non-linear description of gravitational waves remains elusive. This research takes inspiration from the Bondi-Sachs formalism and presents a novel approach by describing geometry through geodesics, which removes the degeneracy between coordinates and the metric. The proposed formalism utilizes infinitesimal spherical triangles as fundamental building blocks to relate geodesic flow bundles to Gaussian curvature, enabling the calculation of geodesics from a curvature field up to second order. This paper outlines the first step of the solution's space-like part, which reduces a high-dimensional problem to a 2D triangulation problem.

In a planar fermion model with four-fermion interactions, we investigate the chiral and superconducting gaps, taking into account the influence of the Dirac cone tilt and the chemical potential. Our research reveals distinct behaviors exhibited by planar fermionic systems. When the effective tilt parameter is less than a certain threshold, approximately 0.55, the superconducting phase persists even for negative superconducting coupling constants. Conversely, for larger tilt parameters and positive superconducting coupling constants, the superconducting phase can still exist but within a more limited range. Moreover, we find that the induction of a superconducting gap is hindered in the presence of a chemical potential, especially when the coupling constant is positive, and an increased chemical potential actually favors the emergence of a metallic phase.

The appearance of power laws in various phenomena, including linguistic patterns and phase transitions, is often discernible when large amounts of data are collected and analyzed accurately. Given the growing scale of neural recordings, researchers are attempting to identify power-law relationships within these datasets. This paper discusses potential pitfalls in detecting power laws in neural data and proposes a Bayesian interpolation framework for this purpose. By applying this framework to synthetic and experimental data from mouse primary visual cortex recordings, our analysis demonstrates that power-law estimates heavily depend on assumed noise models, data ranges, and specific recordings. While our findings support the smoothness of population responses to simple stimuli, they raise doubts about natural images and highlight the need for future research to explore larger data ranges and employ the proposed framework to reevaluate power-law scalings in neural data.

We define a new type of error-correcting code known as LCD subspace codes, which are comprised of nonempty sets of subspaces in a vector space $\mathbb{F}^n_q$. These codes, similar to linear codes with complementary duals, have the unique property that their intersection with their duals is trivial. We demonstrate that the decoding process for an LCD subspace code can be reduced to a simpler form, compared to a general subspace code, specifically under nearest-codeword or maximum-likelihood conditions. Furthermore, under certain conditions, equitable partitions of association schemes yield such LCD subspace codes, and we provide examples from distance-regular graphs as illustrations of this method.

We have calculated the full electroweak radiative corrections of order alpha for Higgs boson production at the ILC, taking into account beam polarization. Utilizing the GRACE-Loop software, we contrasted these results with the effects of factorized initial state radiation to isolate and quantify the weak corrections, which are found to be substantial and essential for precise Higgs boson measurements at ILC.

A cutting-edge forecasting method called PIDD-CG was created to forecast how the probabilities of complex systems change over time, even when only partial data is available. PIDD-CG combines a special statistical model that looks at multiple scales with a highly efficient way to incorporate new data, allowing it to represent probabilities as a mix of different statistics without becoming too complicated for high-dimensional systems. By using a combination of mathematical formulas and neural networks to model the behavior of each possible scenario, PIDD-CG can effectively capture the complex fluctuations in these systems. To further refine this approach, PIDD-CG uses a specific metric to measure the accuracy of the results, allowing it to more precisely forecast the behavior of highly turbulent systems that exhibit frequent and extreme changes.

This study introduces a mathematical framework for a Transactive Memory System (TMS) that influences the collaborative process of learning a skill. The proposed model integrates two key aspects: the individual members' level of expertise and their interaction dynamics. Simulation results demonstrate that if all group members are non-resistant, they can ultimately reach the same level of proficiency as the most experienced group members. In contrast, if all group members are resistant to change, the ability to transfer knowledge depends on the structure of their interaction network.

In today's computing landscape where AI and data processing are shifting towards IoT and edge computing, it is essential to assess the capabilities of devices with limited resources. In this context, Single-Board Computers stand out as versatile and cost-effective systems, with previous studies focusing on high-level benchmarks for specific applications like AI and healthcare. However, there is a need for low-level benchmarking tools and datasets to support the development of new AI-driven solutions for network management and individual device identification, which depend on device and component performance. This paper presents LwHBench, a low-level hardware benchmarking tool designed to measure CPU, GPU, memory, and storage performance on Single-Board Computers, taking into account their specific hardware constraints. LwHBench has been implemented for Raspberry Pi devices and tested on 45 devices for 100 days, generating a comprehensive dataset that enables the application of AI techniques to optimize device management. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the value of the dataset through AI-enabled use cases that explore device identification, performance variability, and the impact of context on device performance. Lastly, the benchmarking tool has been adapted for use in a specific agriculture-focused scenario involving three RockPro64 devices.

This work examines the long-term development of Venus's atmosphere and how its composition is shaped by a continuous exchange between the planet's interior and exterior.  The formation and evolution of Venus's atmosphere, resulting in the current surface conditions, remain topics of intense debate and involve various disciplines. We investigate these interconnected mechanisms, which contributed to the evolution of the atmosphere, by starting with the origins and destinations of volatile elements. Our discussion extends from the planet's interior to the atmosphere, covering volcanic outbursts, interactions between the surface and atmosphere, and atmospheric loss. Furthermore, we delve into more intricate aspects of Venus's past, including the influence of Late Accretion impacts, the link between magnetic field generation and long-term evolution, and the consequences of geochemical and geodynamical feedback cycles for atmospheric development. We propose potential evolutionary paths that Venus may have taken, from its formation to the present day, based on both modeling and observations. Three possible scenarios are considered: one in which atmospheric loss led to the desiccation of the planet during the magma ocean phase, another in which Venus had liquid water on its surface for extended periods, only to enter a runaway greenhouse phase, and a third scenario in which inefficient outgassing kept water within the planet, resulting in the core trapping hydrogen and mantle oxidation. We discuss existing evidence and outline necessary future observations and missions to improve our understanding of Venus's past, the complex feedback cycles operating between the planet's interior, surface, and atmosphere, and their implications for both the past and future of the planet.

This discussion focuses on some lesser-known findings related to marginal log-linear models, and develops novel models that may have applications in mediation analysis within logistic regression. Specifically, we delve into the connection between interaction parameters across different marginal distributions, and present a method for estimating these parameters across various marginals.

The rapid advancements in digital imaging technology have led to an enormous surge in data generated from images, necessitating efficient processing and analysis methods. Given the exceptional accuracy of deep learning algorithms, especially when trained on large datasets, these algorithms are currently the best choice for image analysis. However, their high computational requirements make them resource-intensive, resulting in significant time consumption. Utilizing third-party cloud services can alleviate these demands, but poses significant legal and privacy concerns, particularly when it comes to analyzing medical images, and may not always yield real-time results. This paper proposes an innovative computing architecture that can efficiently analyze medical images in real-time using deep learning without the need to transfer data to a third-party server. To enhance the performance of local image processing on modern multi-core processors, we employ parallel processing to mitigate the resource-intensive demands of deep neural networks. Our focus is on a specific medical-industrial case study - the quantification of blood vessels in microcirculation images, for which we have developed a functioning system. This system is currently used in an industrial, clinical research setting as part of an e-health application, and our results demonstrate that it achieves an impressive 78% speed boost over its serial counterpart, and 12% better performance than a master-slave parallel system architecture.

This work develops a theory of multiplicative connections for specific groupoid mappings and their infinitesimal analogues, along with the construction of barriers to these connections' existence. The theory is further established for various groupoid classes, including all proper ones. The study reveals analogous concepts to principal bundle connections in this broader setup, encompassing 1-forms, curvature 2-forms, and the Bianchi identity. A significant application of this research is presented in [17], showcasing its potential in constructing local models and linearizing around Poisson submanifolds.

Earth surface land cover maps created from Satellite Image Time Series data have become increasingly detailed and accurate over time. These image time series are essential for developing systems that generate precise, up-to-date land cover maps. Various applications utilize these time series, such as mapping ecosystems, monitoring vegetation, and tracking human-induced land use changes. However, recent SITS classification methods often neglect to fully utilize the temporal dimension, resulting in labor-intensive pre-processing and extended training times. This paper aims to improve upon the proposed Temporal CNN method for SITS classification, by implementing and fine-tuning it on existing datasets. Comprehensive experiments on two benchmark datasets showed that Temporal CNNs outperformed or matched benchmark algorithms for both datasets. Moreover, the study highlighted the challenges of optimizing the Temporal CNN architecture for new datasets.

We have developed a novel exact $\gamma=5/3$ spherical accretion solution that corrects the Bondi boundary condition of constant density at large distances to one where density approaches zero at infinity, resulting in physically grounded power law solutions for density and infall velocity fields, encompassing a range of scenarios from free-fall to hydrostatic equilibrium. The solution exhibits a maximum accretion rate and a constant Mach number across the entire flow, unlike the Bondi solution which has a sonic radius. The Bondi solution is shown to converge to our new solution as the source radius approaches zero, justifying its broader applicability. Our solution allows for an analytical exploration of deviations from sphericity using perturbative methods and reveals a rich phenomenology in terms of Legendre polynomials for specific angular velocity boundary conditions, offering valuable physical insights into accretion phenomena.

Evaluating keyword spotting systems that identify specific words in spoken language is complex, particularly under strict data privacy guidelines. Since these systems are designed to collect data only when a specified word is present, it is difficult to obtain sufficient samples for accurate evaluation, making it hard to estimate a model's recall rate. Furthermore, additional data from other sources might not accurately represent the real-world application. To address these challenges, we introduce the AB/BA analysis technique, a framework that compares a candidate model to a baseline model using data from different sources, enabling relative recall rate estimation without requiring negative samples. Additionally, we propose a method for estimating the relative false positive rate between models with minimal variation even when false positives are rare. We also suggest leveraging machine-generated labels to enhance the efficiency, privacy, and cost-effectiveness of the analysis. Our experiments with both simulated and real data demonstrate that the AB/BA analysis technique is effective in measuring improvements in recall rates along with trade-offs in false positive rates.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning, including powerful generative models and
joint text-image representations, have equipped the computational creativity
community with innovative tools, offering fresh avenues for artistic expression.
Text-to-image synthesis approaches that produce images from text inputs are a prime
example. These images are created with an evolving latent vector that is iteratively
refined to align with text descriptions. To achieve this, image patches are randomly
sampled and compared with text prompts in a shared embedding space. The latent
vector is then adjusted using gradient descent to minimize the difference between
image patches and text cues. Although this method grants artists considerable
freedom to customize image aesthetics through generative model selection, its reliance
on a straightforward metric often leads to mode collapse: the entire image is drawn
towards an average representation of all text inputs, losing diversity in the process.
To mitigate this problem, we suggest incorporating techniques from optimal transport
theory, resulting in images that accurately reflect a wide range of input prompts.
We provide numerous visual demonstrations illustrating the benefits of OT in
avoiding limitations associated with mean distance estimates, and show the
superiority of our proposed method in experiments through both qualitative and
quantitative evaluations.

Substantial evidence indicates that cells experiencing fluctuating oxygen levels are more resistant to radiation and, consequently, may significantly influence radiotherapy outcomes, particularly for treatments with fewer sessions. Although hypoxia's impact on radiotherapy has been extensively studied, its cyclic form and the role it plays in radiotherapy efficacy have received relatively little attention. To quantify this effect, a model of cyclic hypoxia was developed in conjunction with a fractionation model to estimate the survival of cancerous cells. By accounting for oxygen transport and fluctuations, it was found that the loss of cell-killing efficiency with increased treatment sessions is not as pronounced as previously assumed. However, ultra-hypofractionated regimens may not fully compensate for this loss, necessitating caution when implementing single-fraction treatments.

Given an analytic set $V$ within a pseudoconvex domain $\Omega$, it is demonstrated that there exists a pseudoconvex domain $G \subseteq \Omega$, encompassing $V$, with the characteristic that every holomorphic function on $V$ that is bounded, can be extended to a bounded holomorphic function on $G$ while retaining the same norm. Furthermore, for certain analytic sets, such a pseudoconvex domain $G$ is specifically identified. Additionally, within the context of an operhedron $\Omega$, it has been shown that there exists a norm on holomorphic functions on $V$ that can always be preserved upon extension to $\Omega$.

Recent studies have demonstrated that for dynamical black holes in higher derivative theories of gravity, a spatial entropy current can be constructed to represent entropy in- and outflow at the horizon, as long as the amplitude's dynamics remain relatively small. This construction, however, heavily relies on the chosen slicing of the horizon along its null generators. Our note reveals that despite changes in the entropy density and spatial current resulting from reparametrization of the null generator, the overall entropy production remains invariant, being the time derivative of the entropy density plus the divergence of the spatial current. This claim has been explicitly confirmed in the specific case of Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet dynamical black holes theory.

A practical approach for integrating quantum computing capabilities into personal edge devices lies in using simple devices with low error tolerance that offload computational tasks to more advanced quantum computers through edge servers equipped with cryogenic components and fault-tolerant systems. This setup allows network elements to use various encoding protocols. A new proposal for achieving mobile edge-quantum computing involves developing quantum terminals that are compatible with a range of encoding formats. By placing an atomic lattice processor inside a cavity and utilizing Rydberg-Fermi cavity-QED technology, entanglement is facilitated. A specific gate operation enables quantum qubits to become entangled through the interaction of Rydberg electrons with plaquette atoms. This results in various arrangements of logical qubits with distinguishable eigenstates and photon emission characteristics. Applying an entanglement-swapping gate to photons emitted by the process enables the entanglement of distant qubits regardless of the encoding protocol they use. This universal photonic interface can be used to link and cluster processors with quantum memories and the quantum cloud while accommodating different encoding formats.

A novel method for risk-sensitive control of partially observable linear systems affected by process and measurement noise is presented. The proposed control strategy incorporates two risk constraints, enabling it to mitigate variability induced by the noises. By limiting the statistical variability of both state and output predictions, this formulation develops a risk-averse control policy. Characteristic of linear quadratic control, the proposed optimal policy retains its favorable properties and is represented by an affine function of minimum mean square error estimates. The linear component of the policy strictly regulates states in directions prone to large process and measurement noise, noise covariance, cross-covariance, and corresponding penalties. The affine terms force the states against higher-order noise statistics. Moreover, this policy is computationally efficient, enabling pre-computation offline, thereby avoiding prior method limitations. Additionally, a stability analysis confirms that the derived controller is internally stable across various parameter settings. The effectiveness of the proposed control policy is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

The discovery of gravitational wave astronomy has provided a means to evaluate the validity of modified theories of gravity that attempt to explain dark energy. In specific dilaton models, differences in inferred distances to cosmic sources based on both electromagnetic and gravitational wave observations would arise due to the presence of a damping effect. These theories suggest a variable relationship between Newton's constant and the fine structure constant over time. This study investigates the potential to verify these models. By detecting collocated sources such as supernovae and neutron star mergers using both electromagnetic telescopes and gravitational wave detectors, researchers can determine whether light and gravitational waves are subject to the same propagation laws across vast distances, ultimately constraining the time-variable ratio of Newton's constant to the fine structure constant. Next-generation gravitational wave detectors in conjunction with future observatories will enable the detection or constraint of these variations to within a few parts in 100. We apply this method to the GW170817 event, using distances measured by the LIGO and Virgo detectors and the observed Kilonova.

This study presents cosmological solutions that accurately describe the universe's current accelerating expansion phase, utilizing a geometrical scalar-tensor theory of gravity within the context of Weyl's integrable geometry. By adopting a power law expansion in a Weyl scalar field and an invariant metric, we identified a class of power law solutions, which align with PLANCK 2018 data for specific model parameters. The model's deceleration parameter converges asymptotically to $-1/2$, consistent with observational evidence.

The uncertainty surrounding the size of the dust particles in planet-forming disks poses significant challenges to understanding the collisional growth of these aggregates. Despite its importance, the size of the monomers within dust aggregates has yet to be effectively constrained by disk observations. A study aims to rectify this uncertainty by deriving the monomer size using data from optical and near-infrared polarimetric observations of planet-forming disks. A thorough investigation into the effects of monomer size, aggregate size, porosity, and composition on the degree of linear polarization of scattered light was conducted using the T-matrix method. By comparing the results with observed polarization fractions from several planet-forming disks, it was found that the monomer size has a significant impact on the degree of polarization when its size parameter is larger than one or two. Notably, the study suggests that the monomer radius does not exceed 0.4 micrometers, aligning with subunit sizes of the solar system's dust aggregates and interstellar grains. These findings indicate that optical and near-infrared polarimetric observations can serve as a valuable tool in determining the initial conditions necessary for dust coagulation and planetesimal formation in planet-forming disks.

This paper delves into the concept of herdability in linear time-invariant state-space models. We examine the ability of these systems to steer towards positive states based on matrix pairs (A,B), where A represents a multi-agent network and B designates a subset of leaders. The conditions for herdability in networks with directed clustering, structurally balanced structures, and tree topologies, particularly when there is only one leader, are specifically analyzed.

The analysis of the fingerprinting game is conducted under the assumption that the tracer knows the coalition size $k$, but the colluders can distribute themselves across $L$ TV channels. We introduce the collusion channel to illustrate the additional degrees of freedom the coalition possesses in our model. We formulate a payoff function similar to the one used in the single channel scenario, and hypothesize that it closely relates to the fingerprinting capacity. For a binary alphabet case under the marking assumption and a one channel per person per segment constraint, we determine the asymptotic behavior of the payoff function. As a result, we find that the maximin value of the game for our payoff function converges to $L^2/k^2 \cdot 2 \ln 2$. Furthermore, we identify the optimal strategy for the tracer as the arcsine distribution and for the coalition as the interleaving attack strategy across all TV channels, along with evenly distributing the colluders across $L$ TV channels.

The dynamics of general relativity can be obtained from various actions that differ from the Einstein-Hilbert action and use different variables to describe motion. Among these alternatives is the teleparallel equivalent, a torsion-based theory grounded in the tetrad field. More comprehensive torsion-based models have emerged in recent years with the intention of supplanting general relativity. There are currently two primary methods of formulating these theories; one employs a spin connection, and the other does not. This discussion will focus on the concept of Lorentz gauge invariance within these theories, and a fundamental yet concise proof will be provided that both formulations are inherently equivalent.

This paper establishes tight generalization error upper limits for deep neural networks that process datasets structured by Markov chains. Building on Koltchinskii and Panchenko's work on classifier generalization error bounds for i.i.d. data, our research introduces new inequalities in high-dimensional probability for Markov chains. A key component in these inequalities is the spectral gap of the infinitesimal generator of the Markov chain. Moreover, we present an efficient method for converting traditional generalization error bounds in deep learning and machine learning to their Bayesian equivalents for both i.i.d. and Markov datasets, as well as extend this framework to more complex Markov models and datasets composed of multiple Markov components.
